title: Every E-Commerce Company Now Sells Goods From Abroad. Can Amazon Use Cross-Border Shopping to Restart Its China Business?
excerpt: China is such a brutal market that no one will stand still and wait for you to grow up.
body:
China is such a brutal market that no one will stand still and wait for you to grow up.

There may be many days in the year that are bad for reading, but very few left that are bad for shopping.

With 6·18 around the corner, the mid-year e-commerce sales season started as early as the end of May. In past years Amazon China followed JD.com and Tmall into price wars. This year, for the first time, it is flying the banner of "overseas hot items," trying to take the special lane of "haitao" (buying goods from overseas) through Chinese e-commerce's mid-year exam.

Amazon China's sales event is themed "2015 International Brand Oscars." The lineup leads with selected items from Amazon's US site, backed by overseas brands it partners with exclusively, plus food and liquor bought in bulk abroad and shipped to China for sale.

This is not the first time Amazon China has built a promotion around overseas shopping. Last August, [it announced a partnership with the Shanghai Free Trade Zone](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/1966.html). Two months later, Amazon said its sites in six countries would [ship directly to Chinese customers](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/3148.html), and soon after it [launched a Chinese-language overseas shopping site for Singles' Day](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/3419.html), bringing America's "Black Friday" to Chinese e-commerce.

Amazon China now helps users shop overseas in two ways. One is "Global Store" on the Chinese Amazon site. The other is "direct import sourcing": it buys in bulk at the source overseas, stores the goods in its fulfillment centers, and sells them directly from inside China.

This March, Amazon even [opened a flagship store on its rival Tmall](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/7166.html), selling goods bought in bulk overseas.

## What Amazon China Has Done to Help You Shop Overseas

Amazon's Tianjin fulfillment center, in the Wuqing Development Zone, opened in 2012. Covering more than 90,000 square meters, it is Amazon's largest fulfillment center in China. Every day, once they clear customs, a large share of the goods Chinese Amazon users buy from Amazon's US site through "Global Store" are sent here for sorting, then shipped on to smaller fulfillment centers around the country or straight to customers.

The Tianjin center has set aside a space the size of two basketball courts just for "Global Store" goods. Once the goods are packed and shipped from Amazon US warehouses, all they need here is a Chinese shipping label that the system has matched in advance, and they can enter Amazon's ordinary shipping process.

![Global Store parcels being processed at Amazon's Tianjin fulfillment center](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121401TZrOvmHMuaIEARfD.jpg-w600)

Goods that come in through Global Store carry black tape, which sets them apart from Amazon China's own inventory. Amazon US recently [printed a full-panel Minions ad](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/10434.html) on its shipping boxes, so these black-taped Minions boxes have also crossed the ocean with Global Store orders to fulfillment centers in Tianjin, Shanghai and elsewhere.

![Black-taped Minions shipping boxes from Amazon US](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121401CsqXHPGYO2F6o9bi.jpg-w600)

According to operations manager Guan Yuehong (Amy), goods that have cleared customs and arrived from the customs office must be processed within 24 hours. To manage this, the Tianjin center designed its own radial sorting station, which staff call the "octopus." By three or four in the afternoon, the last batch from the previous day usually has to be finished; by five or six in the evening, a new batch of cleared boxes arrives.

![The radial "octopus" sorting station at the Tianjin fulfillment center](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121402PSsVzcuADfxt7XkY.jpg-w600)

## Ten Years in China, Amazon China Finally Looks a Little Different

Over the past year, the word "haitao" has gradually given way to "cross-border e-commerce," because more and more e-commerce platforms now treat "going abroad to buy things that are hard to find in China" as serious business. You could say Amazon China has finally found a direction where it has the edge, or you could say this wave of e-commerce enthusiasm has finally run into Amazon's strengths.

According to a Nielsen survey, mainland China has at least 18 million overseas shoppers, who spent as much as US$213.6 billion abroad in the past 12 months.

Amazon cannot fail to see what these numbers mean. [Zhao Li, the product manager in charge of Amazon China's "Global Store" project, told QDaily in her Beijing office](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/3941.html): "Amazon US's data show more and more Chinese IP addresses visiting Amazon US."

Since Doug Gurr became president of Amazon China last August, the company, which had always seemed a little sluggish, has finally given the impression that it wants to do something. In 2014, the [number of press releases](http://www.amazon.cn/gp/press/home/2014) it sent to the media rose 61% from 2013. In the same year it held roughly more press conferences about its "international brand strategy" than in the previous several years combined.

Over the past decade, Amazon has built 12 fulfillment centers in China with a combined floor area of more than 500,000 square meters, its largest operations network outside the United States.

Of Amazon China's three presidents, Gurr knows the global business best. He has won Amazon China more autonomy[, as Amazon China vice president Niu Yinghua said in an interview this year](http://www.ebrun.com/20150526/135135.shtml): "He must be an important person, to make all of this happen."

He is also the most publicly active China president Amazon has had. Gurr joined Amazon in 2011 to run its UK business and a year later was promoted to head Amazon Europe. Compared with his predecessor, Feng Enzhe, Gurr has brought more visible change and has a stronger presence.

So far this year, Gurr has published two bylined articles on cross-border e-commerce, setting out Amazon China's plan to bring international products into China through three models: "Global Store," "overseas direct sourcing" and "free trade zone cooperation."

"Global Store" is the part of its cross-border strategy that Amazon China has put the most effort into. From an initial small media briefing, to the announcement of a trial launch and then the official launch, to a report on its first half-year results this May, Amazon has held four press conferences for this one project.

![Amazon China press conference for Black Friday](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121402TxUMAPfO2QVjS6ba.jpg-w600)

Last November, Amazon China held several press conferences for Black Friday

When the trial began, Zhao Li and her "Global Store" product team picked best-selling items in seven categories that Chinese overseas shoppers often buy, including mother and baby, footwear and outdoor gear, translated the product descriptions into Chinese, and added them to the "Global Store" section.

On Amazon China's website, users can see in real time the details and stock levels of products on Amazon US, with prices converted into yuan at the current exchange rate. On the Chinese site, you search for and select an item marked "Global Store," read the Chinese description, choose to buy, log in with an Amazon US account, set an address and pay by credit card. That completes the order.

The range has since grown to 24 categories, and the Global Store team expects that by the end of June the site will cover every category Amazon US now carries. Zhang Saying, the vice president in charge of public relations, said: "Only one is left."

Amazon's overseas sites have taken part as well. Zhang Saying told QDaily that because suppliers already work with Amazon's local teams, the whole procurement process has been cut to a single step: the supplier ticks one box in its contract with Amazon US, "agree to sell products outside the United States." The products can then go live on "Global Store," and Chinese users can buy them on an all-Chinese page.

From the time the China team proposed Global Store last March to the trial launch in November, more than 100 Amazon teams around the world were involved, along with more than 100 people in China. Zhao Li said that for a multinational like Amazon, this speed was unprecedented, and the project has a high priority inside the company.

Meanwhile, the "overseas direct sourcing" project, prepared since 2013 and launched in stages, has gradually caught consumers' attention. "Global Store" relies on Amazon US's resources. With "overseas direct sourcing," Amazon China sends its own team to import goods in bulk from where they are made, and users can buy them directly on z.cn.

QDaily has previously been invited to visit Amazon's Beijing and Tianjin fulfillment centers. At both, the "overseas direct sourcing" goods (mainly food and wine) have their own zones, kept apart from ordinary goods from the moment they reach the staging area to wait for shelving. At the Beijing center, our reporter saw shelves built specially for imported wine, which hold the bottles at a tilt so the corks stay wet.

![Custom shelves holding imported wine at a tilt in Amazon's Beijing fulfillment center](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121403XU9RxsTSapOiMDun.jpg-w600)

## The Giants Pile Into Cross-Border E-Commerce

Nielsen's survey data show that more than 50% of Chinese overseas shoppers visited Amazon's "Global Store" in the past six months.

This is Amazon's eleventh year in China, and it seems to have finally found a way to compete that sets it apart from other e-commerce platforms. This may well be Amazon's last chance to turn things around in China.

Data from iResearch show that last year China's cross-border e-commerce grew by an average of about 30%, far faster than traditional offline foreign trade. The Ministry of Commerce forecasts that in 2016, the total value of China's cross-border e-commerce imports and exports will reach 6.5 trillion yuan.

This market has always been there. Domestic e-commerce companies have joined in too, using it to stand out. After all, rather than straining to be "cheaper than you" on the same products, it is better to find exclusive supply overseas and be the one that "has what you don't."

Just as Taobao invented Singles' Day out of nothing, [JD.com, which single-handedly created the "6·18" sales event](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/10763.html), this year for the first time gave "global shopping" a place in the main 6·18 promotion. Of course, JD.com has been preparing for this day for a long time.

In the first quarter of this year, Liu Qiangdong led a JD.com delegation to France and South Korea to open up markets, launching a France Pavilion, a Korea Pavilion and a Japan Pavilion in turn. Next on the JD Global team's list are Australia, the United States and other major European countries.

In April, JD Global officially launched, and 150,000 international products from 1,200 brands entered the JD Global channel by two routes: JD's own purchasing, and overseas brands signing up to open their own stores.

[On the other side, Tmall announced at the end of May the launch of its "Tmall X strategy"](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/9985.html). Besides teaming up with several brands on a "Super Brand Day," more than 20,000 merchants on Tmall are taking part in this mid-year sale, offering imported goods from 25 countries. Featured products from a group of top global supermarkets will be priced about the same as in their home countries, or even lower, and, as on Singles' Day, Tmall will offer "free worldwide shipping, bonded."

A year earlier, Alibaba had launched a dedicated overseas shopping channel, "Tmall Global." By February this year, 5,400 overseas brands from 25 countries and regions had set up shop on Tmall.

![Tmall Global's overseas shopping promotion](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726135606oc45ZEr8hyb0fWRY.jpg-w600)

Zhixing, head of merchant recruitment at Tmall Global, told QDaily that it admits merchants by invitation only, and has offered KA (Key Account) service since last year. When recruiting, besides finding merchants, it assigns locals or Chinese staff, depending on the merchant's region, to guide them and make sure they actually get set up.

Before Alibaba's listing last year, a New York Times commentary said that "[Alibaba is the driver of luxury consumption by China's middle class](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/2323.html)." On Tmall, major brands can sell directly to customers. How well Alibaba keeps this promise will decide how far it can open up the vast Chinese market, so that global retailers and ambitious small and medium-sized businesses can get a share.

If you remember how Tmall last month [copied the hype used to sell iPhones](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/9305.html) to sell apples from New Zealand, it is not hard to see why this platform, which controls 58.6% of China's e-commerce business, will be a formidable opponent.

## Amazon Has Changed a Lot in China, but Perhaps Not Enough

Amazon is the name overseas brands know better, and they often already work with it. JD.com and Alibaba may struggle negotiating with suppliers one by one around the world; the suppliers Amazon has built up globally give it a strong hand to play in cross-border e-commerce.

Introducing the "overseas direct sourcing" project to QDaily, Niu Yinghua said that brands little known in China are willing to bring their products to China through Amazon's platform because of their long relationships with Amazon.

In the past, more than half of all individual overseas shopping took place on Amazon's sites around the world. Now that Amazon is doing this itself and helping users past the language barrier, the people hit hardest are small-scale personal shoppers who buy on others' behalf. Amazon plans to bring goods from its German, Spanish, Japanese and other sites onto "Global Store" the same way, and then its advantage across languages will become even clearer.

The question is whether the first suppliers, each won on a platform's own merits, will keep working with it after a while. Whether it is the international Amazon, the local Alibaba or JD.com, or even a small e-commerce site focused on a niche, the only thing that keeps suppliers on board is who can bring them more stable sales.

Is Amazon China's effort enough to take on these rivals?

"It took Amazon a long time to realize that copying the Amazon US model does not work in China," Amazon China president Doug Gurr once told Bloomberg Businessweek (Chinese edition).

For the previous decade, Amazon did try to repeat in China the path that had worked at home.

In 2004, Amazon entered China by buying the online bookseller Joyo. As in the United States, Amazon hoped to build shopping habits in China starting with books, and then expand into more categories.

But Taobao/Tmall and JD.com, which ended up winning the most online shoppers in China, got their start selling women's clothing and electronics respectively.

Not until October 2011 was Joyo Amazon formally renamed "Amazon China," with the short domain z.cn. The ads promoting z.cn were almost the only offline exposure Amazon's e-commerce business got in ten years. After that, the e-commerce business never again got an advertising budget.

In the United States, Amazon has taken on one new field after another; in 2014 alone it spent more than US$2.4 billion on digital content. Amazon China, meanwhile, still has no plans to advertise in the subway.

Within a few years, Amazon [used the Kindle to upend the books, music and video business it was founded on](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/8962.html), and Amazon Web Services (AWS), which began as a way to pull together product catalog data, has grown into [a business with annual revenue of US$5 billion](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/9501.html). But all these breakthroughs happened in the United States; the Chinese market did not get the same attention.

After the acquisition, without a steady "blood transfusion" from headquarters, Joyo Amazon lost its chance to knock out Dangdang in the free-shipping war. The Kindle appeared on the support page of Amazon China's website under the name "Jindu" as early as 2010, but only made a "soft landing" as an e-book store in December 2012, more than five years after the first Kindle went on sale in the United States.

Competition in e-commerce is even fiercer. In 2014, JD.com and Alibaba listed in the United States one after the other. Gurr took up his post just as JD.com was going public in the US. According to JD.com's financial report, its annual sales were about a quarter of Amazon's global sales over the same period, while according to the research firm iResearch, Amazon China's market share is only about a tenth of JD.com's.

![Amazon China fulfillment center](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702121403P9WS6HFcdp0h8Blo.jpg-w600)

Most of Amazon's investment in China has gone where consumers can hardly see it, such as building warehouses and logistics. It has built in China an operations network second only to North America's. [Song Liyuan, vice president of Amazon China, told QDaily](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/9491.html) that it can already deliver the same day or the next day in 135 cities. But that does not solve the problem of a website with no traffic.

Meanwhile, JD.com and Alibaba seemed to enter cross-border e-commerce overnight and grew it fast. JD.com, Tmall, Yihaodian and even small specialist e-commerce platforms have spent heavily to cover subways, buses and office-building light boxes with ads for their products.

In the past couple of days, Alibaba even turned Weibo's home page into an entrance to Tmall's sale, and while people were exclaiming that "Weibo's home page has turned into Tmall," it had already won the exposure and traffic it wanted.

A month before 6·18, JD.com had already put Liu Qiangdong's face in every corner of China's big cities. Amazon, by contrast, does almost no offline promotion and seldom publicizes a product or business before it launches.

Years of aggressive promotion and spending have taught users to shop on Tmall and JD.com. Users are used to opening JD.com or Tmall to buy things, so for these two, entering cross-border e-commerce is like a shop people visit every day putting new goods on its shelves. Amazon has to start by drawing a crowd to a shop that has just opened.

In every niche, especially mother and baby, footwear and fashion, where Amazon China is stronger, a group of small and medium-sized specialist cross-border e-commerce companies has charged into the market backed by investments ranging from tens of millions to more than 100 million US dollars.

And Tmall does not even have to reach out to every merchant itself. Its huge traffic gives overseas Chinese a reason to act as go-betweens, especially in popular areas like mother and baby. Mr. Ni, who is in Australia approaching milk-powder brands and preparing to help them join this year's Singles' Day, told QDaily: "The barrier is very low now. If we register a company overseas, we can get onto Tmall Global."

The Shanghai Free Trade Zone has lowered the cost for small and medium-sized brands to enter China. Merchants selling on Tmall can first ship their Singles' Day stock to a bonded warehouse in the zone and pay duties only when the goods ship to customers.

## The Competition Is Not Only About "Selling Things"

Yet competition over buying and selling is not the scariest part.

Alibaba, JD.com and even WeChat have all moved into internet finance. That is where these competitors' real killer move lies.

These newcomers to internet finance use credit products such as Huabei and Baitiao to pay for pushing people to spend. If you buy an electric toothbrush on Tmall Global or JD Global, you don't even need a credit card, and you can start paying in installments 50 days later.

[The more users spend, the larger their credit limit and installment discounts](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/10412.html). It is a loop, and that is how shopping works: once you start, you can't stop. It resembles Amazon's Prime membership in the United States, which wins users over with shipping, discounted goods and digital services. Over the past year, Prime membership worldwide rose by nearly 50%, one of the main reasons Amazon's share price has soared in recent months.

Competition among Chinese e-commerce companies has already spread from e-commerce into financial services. Amazon China may need more autonomy, more freedom and more attention from Amazon headquarters.

In this important and fiercely competitive Chinese market, Amazon feels it has changed a great deal.

The Chinese market is not just one part of the Asia-Pacific market. Over the past decade, it has produced more technology companies worth over US$10 billion than anywhere outside the United States. For such a brutal market, [Uber is planning to raise US$1 billion](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/10625.html), all of it to be spent in China. Amazon's investment in China is still far from enough.

Cover image: Amazon

(Xu Bingqing also contributed to this article)
